kurzfassung: John R. Miles talks with actor, entrepreneur, and father Josh Duhamel about how his cabin in Minnesota and rural roots helped him slow down and reconnect with himself. They discuss the realities of parenting at different life stages, shifting away from external validation and ego, and why he co-founded the wellness company Gatlin. The conversation also covers his upcoming projects, including Ransom Canyon, The Rescue, and Runaway.
stichpunkte: Josh Duhamel explains that spending time at his cabin in rural Minnesota significantly lowers his heart rate and grounds him.
He reflects on the differences between raising his 12-year-old son and his younger children, noting how much parenting technology has advanced.
Physical labor, building trails, and handling heavy machinery provide him with a sense of purpose and presence that acting does not.
He shares his fascination with off-the-grid living, preparedness, and the ongoing development of his property.
Aging and experience helped him realize that his past struggles with identity were rooted in ego and insecurity rather than external pressure.
He discusses co-founding the telemedicine and wellness company Gatlin to make testosterone replacement therapy and peptide optimization accessible for men.
He defines true success not by material achievement, but by family memories and the legacy he leaves for his children.
He mentions his recent and upcoming work, including Netflix's Ransom Canyon, The Rescue, and Runaway.
beschreibung:
What would change if you stopped worrying so much about what everyone else thinks of you?

Actor, entrepreneur, and father Josh Duhamel has spent decades in the spotlight, but he says one of the biggest things he has learned with age is that he no longer needs to pretend for anyone—and that caring too much about other people's opinions once kept him from living his “full version” of himself.

In this deeply personal conversation, John R. Miles sits down with the actor, entrepreneur, and father to talk about identity, success, fatherhood, presence, and what it means to build a life that actually feels like your own.

Josh opens up about:

Why success doesn't automatically make you feel like you've done enough

How the need for validation can keep you chasing the next achievement

What helped him stop caring so much about other people's opinions

Why his cabin in Minnesota brings out a different version of himself

How changing his environment helped him become more present

Why fatherhood completely changed his definition of success

What he hopes his children remember about him

Why family memories now matter more to him than material success

How he's learning to embrace simplicity, curiosity, and being present

One of the most revealing moments comes when Josh talks about what success means to him now. Despite everything he has accomplished, he admits that he still feels like he has more to prove and achieve.
